articles.law: AMA Short-Term Rental Framework (Law 4472/2017 as amended)
articles.title: Definition and Scope of Short-Term Rental
articles.compliance_check: Applies to all short-term rental listings in Greece regardless of property type or size.
articles.body: Short-term rental (STR) in Greece is defined as the furnished letting of a residential property for a period of fewer than 365 consecutive days to the same tenant, through digital platforms. Any property listed on a digital platform such as Airbnb, Booking.com or similar services falls under this framework. The property owner (host) is classified as either a natural person or a legal entity. Properties subject to this law include entire apartments, houses, rooms within a primary residence, and any furnished residential space offered commercially for short stays.

articles.law: AMA Short-Term Rental Framework (Law 4472/2017 as amended)
articles.title: Mandatory AADE Registration and License Number
articles.compliance_check: License field is empty or missing (has_license == False). This is the most fundamental compliance violation.
articles.penalty: Fine of €5,000 per unlicensed property per calendar year (increased to €10,000 for repeat violations).
articles.body: All short-term rental properties in Greece must be registered with the Independent Authority for Public Revenue (AADE — Ανεξάρτητη Αρχή Δημοσίων Εσόδων) before being listed on any digital platform. Upon registration, the AADE issues a unique Short-Term Rental Registration Number (AΜΕΑ — Αριθμός Μητρώου Ενοικιαζόμενης Ακινήτου). This number must be prominently displayed on every online listing. A listing without a valid AADE registration number is operating illegally. The registration must be renewed annually and kept up to date. Failure to register prior to listing constitutes a primary violation of Greek short-term rental law.

articles.law: AMA Short-Term Rental Framework (Law 4472/2017 as amended)
articles.title: Night Cap — Primary vs Secondary Residence
articles.compliance_check: If estimated_occupancy_l365d implies more than 90 nights AND the property is a secondary home, a tax compliance review is triggered.
articles.penalty: Tax surcharge of 15–30% on undeclared rental income plus interest. Criminal prosecution possible for repeated or deliberate violations.
articles.body: Greek law distinguishes between a primary residence and a secondary property for short-term rental purposes. A natural person may rent their primary residence (or a room within it) for up to 90 nights per calendar year without additional tax obligations. If the annual rental nights exceed 90 for a primary residence, or if the property is a secondary residence used for commercial rental purposes, the income is classified as business income and subject to full business taxation. Properties rented for more than 90 nights per year must also file a special STR income declaration. Exceeding the 90-night threshold without proper business registration constitutes a tax compliance violation.

articles.law: AMA Short-Term Rental Framework (Law 4472/2017 as amended)
articles.title: Tax Declaration Obligations for Hosts
articles.compliance_check: Applies to all active listings generating rental income. Cross-referenced with estimated_revenue_l365d.
articles.penalty: Penalty of 25–100% of undeclared tax liability. Listings operating without tax declaration are subject to immediate suspension.
articles.body: All rental income derived from short-term rentals must be declared in the host's annual personal income tax return (E1 form). The income must also be declared in the special short-term rental property declaration (E2 form) filed with AADE. Hosts earning rental income above €12,000 per year from short-term rentals are subject to VAT registration obligations. Income from short-term rentals is subject to personal income tax at graduated rates: 15% up to €12,000, 35% for €12,001–35,000, and 45% above €35,000. All hosts operating on digital platforms must also submit quarterly income summaries through the myDATA digital accounting system.

articles.law: AMA Short-Term Rental Framework (Law 4472/2017 as amended)
articles.title: Platform Obligations — Display of Registration Number
articles.compliance_check: If license field exists but is malformed or absent from the listing display, this article applies.
articles.penalty: Platform fines of up to €500,000 per quarter for systematic non-compliance. Individual listing suspension.
articles.body: Digital platforms facilitating short-term rentals in Greece (including Airbnb, Booking.com, Vrbo, and any comparable service) are legally required to display the AADE short-term rental registration number on each listing page. Platforms must verify the validity of the registration number before publishing a listing. Platforms that knowingly list unregistered properties are subject to regulatory fines. The registration number must appear in a standardised format (e.g., '00XXXXXXXXX') in the listing description or a dedicated compliance field. As of 2023, AADE conducts quarterly cross-checks of platform listing data against its registration database.

articles.law: AMA Short-Term Rental Framework (Law 4472/2017 as amended)
articles.title: Multiple Property Restriction and Professional Host Classification
articles.compliance_check: host_total_listings_count >= 3 AND host_type is natural person (non-business). Triggers professional operator classification review.
articles.penalty: Reclassification as commercial accommodation operator. Fines of €20,000–€100,000 for operating as unlicensed commercial accommodation.
articles.body: A natural person (individual, non-business entity) may operate a maximum of 2 short-term rental properties under the simplified AMA framework. Operating 3 or more properties as a natural person requires formal business registration as a STR operator, VAT registration, and compliance with commercial accommodation regulations (Law 4276/2014). Hosts managing 3 or more listings are classified as professional operators regardless of whether the properties are owned, co-owned, or managed under a property management agreement. Professional operators are subject to additional safety inspections, fire safety compliance, and accessible accommodation regulations.

articles.law: AMA Short-Term Rental Framework (Law 4472/2017 as amended)
articles.title: Health, Safety and Building Compliance
articles.compliance_check: Applies to all registered properties. Cannot be directly verified from listing data alone — requires physical inspection.
articles.penalty: Suspension of registration and listing. Fines of €3,000–€15,000 for safety non-compliance.
articles.body: All short-term rental properties in Greece must meet minimum health and safety standards including: functioning smoke detectors, carbon monoxide detectors, fire extinguisher on each floor, first aid kit, emergency exit signage for multi-storey buildings, and safe electrical installations. Properties must be structurally sound with valid building permits. Properties built without legal permits (authentically known as 'arbitrary buildings') may not be legally registered for short-term rental. Building permit compliance is verified during AADE registration. The municipality may conduct spot inspections of registered STR properties for safety compliance.

articles.law: Loi Le Meur (Law No. 2024-1039, November 2024) — Loi visant à remédier aux déséquilibres du marché locatif
articles.title: Definition and Scope — Short-Term Furnished Rental
articles.compliance_check: Applies to all short-term rental listings in France regardless of property type.
articles.body: The Loi Le Meur (Law 2024-1039 of 19 November 2024) governs the rental of furnished residential accommodation for short durations in France. It defines a short-term furnished rental (MEUBLÉ DE TOURISME) as any furnished residential property rented to transient guests for periods of fewer than 90 consecutive days per occupant. This law applies to all properties listed on digital platforms such as Airbnb, Booking.com, Abritel, Vrbo, or any equivalent service. The law applies throughout France but grants municipalities — particularly large urban agglomerations such as Paris, Lyon, Bordeaux, and Nice — enhanced powers to impose additional local restrictions. Paris is subject to the most stringent application of this law.

articles.title: Primary Residence — 120-Night Annual Cap
articles.compliance_check: If estimated_occupancy_l365d implies more than 120 occupied nights AND the property is a primary residence, cap violation is triggered.
articles.penalty: Administrative fine of up to €10,000 per property. Platforms face fines of up to €50,000 for failing to enforce the cap.
articles.body: A host may rent their primary residence as a short-term furnished rental for a maximum of 120 nights per calendar year. This limit applies regardless of the number of individual rentals or guests within those nights. A primary residence is defined as the property in which the host resides for at least 8 months per year. If a host exceeds the 120-night annual limit for their primary residence, the excess rental nights are treated as commercial activity and subject to business taxation. Platforms such as Airbnb are legally required to block listings from accepting new bookings once the 120-night cap has been reached. Paris had previously enforced a 120-night cap under local regulation; the Loi Le Meur now makes this a national statutory limit.

articles.title: Secondary Residence — Mandatory Change of Use Authorisation
articles.compliance_check: If the property is not a primary residence AND it has high year-round availability (suggesting commercial secondary use), a changement d'usage review is triggered.
articles.penalty: Fine of up to €50,000 per property. Mandatory reversion to residential use. The municipality may compel the owner to pay €1,000 per day per square metre until the property is returned to residential use.
articles.body: A secondary residence (any property that is not the host's primary residence) may only be used as a short-term furnished rental if the owner has obtained a formal 'changement d'usage' authorisation from the municipality. In Paris, such authorisations are subject to strict quotas and are not freely available. Paris introduced a compensation requirement: for each residential unit converted to tourist use, the owner must convert an equivalent commercial space back to residential use in the same arrondissement (the 'one-for-one' rule). Properties in Paris operating as secondary-residence STRs without a valid changement d'usage authorisation are operating in breach of both the Loi Le Meur and Paris municipal regulations. Secondary-residence STRs are not subject to the 120-night cap — they require the full changement d'usage and are treated as commercial accommodation.

articles.title: Mandatory Registration Number and Platform Display
articles.compliance_check: License field is empty or missing (has_license == False or license is null). Primary compliance violation.
articles.penalty: Fine of up to €5,000 per unlicensed listing. Platforms face fines of €12,500 per non-compliant listing discovered during regulatory inspection.
articles.body: All short-term furnished rental properties in France must be registered with the local municipality (mairie) and obtain a local registration number. In Paris, this registration is mandatory and issued by the City of Paris. The registration number must be displayed prominently in every online listing. Platforms are legally required to verify registration numbers and to remove listings that do not display a valid number. The Loi Le Meur strengthens existing registration requirements by mandating cross-checks between platform data and municipal registration databases. As of 2025, platforms must submit quarterly listing inventories to municipalities for verification. A listing without a valid registration number is in primary violation of French STR law.

articles.title: Municipal Veto Powers and Quota Zones
articles.compliance_check: Listings in high-density Paris neighbourhoods (1st–8th arrondissements) with high STR concentration should be flagged for quota zone review.
articles.penalty: Forced delisting from all platforms. Fines of up to €20,000 per property in a prohibited zone.
articles.body: The Loi Le Meur grants municipalities in France the power to designate specific zones where short-term rentals are prohibited or subject to strict quotas. In Paris, the city council may designate any arrondissement or neighbourhood as a 'zone réglementée' where no new short-term rental authorisations will be granted. Existing authorisations in quota zones may be subject to non-renewal. The law also allows municipalities to set a maximum percentage of residential units in any building that may be converted to short-term rental use. Building co-ownership assemblies (copropriétés) may now ban STR activity in their buildings by a simple majority vote, overriding individual owner rights. Listings in Paris must therefore also comply with the rules of the building in which the property is located.

articles.title: Revised Tax Treatment — Removal of Fiscal Advantage for Meublés de Tourisme
articles.compliance_check: If estimated_revenue_l365d > 15000 AND the listing is non-classified, a tax regime review is triggered.
articles.penalty: Back-payment of taxes, penalties of 10–80% of underpaid tax, plus interest. Potential criminal prosecution for deliberate under-declaration.
articles.body: The Loi Le Meur significantly reduced the tax advantages previously available to furnished tourist rentals (meublés de tourisme) under the micro-BIC fiscal regime. Before the law, STR income was eligible for a 71% flat-rate deduction (abattement) under micro-BIC, compared to 50% for unfurnished residential rentals. The Loi Le Meur reduced the STR micro-BIC abattement to 30% (non-classified meublés de tourisme) or 50% (classified meublés de tourisme with an official rating). The income ceiling for micro-BIC eligibility for non-classified STRs was also reduced from €77,700 to €15,000 per year. Hosts earning more than €15,000 per year in rental income from non-classified STRs must now use the réel simplifié accounting regime, requiring formal accounts and VAT registration. This change has significant implications for high-revenue Paris listings.

articles.title: Platform Obligations — Booking Cap Enforcement and Data Sharing
articles.compliance_check: If a listing lacks a registration number displayed on the platform, the platform is in breach of this article in addition to the host.
articles.penalty: Platform fines of €125,000–€500,000 per quarter depending on scale of non-compliance.
articles.body: Digital platforms facilitating short-term rentals in France bear direct legal responsibility for enforcing the regulatory framework. Specific platform obligations under the Loi Le Meur include: (1) Automatic blocking of bookings once a primary-residence listing reaches 120 nights per year; (2) Verification and display of the municipal registration number for each listing; (3) Refusal to list properties in municipal prohibition zones; (4) Transmission of quarterly booking data to the Direction Générale des Finances Publiques (DGFiP) for tax cross-checking; (5) Transmission of listing inventories to municipalities for quota monitoring. Platforms that fail to comply face regulatory fines and potential suspension of operating licences in France. Airbnb was fined in 2024 for systematic non-compliance with pre-Loi Le Meur registration display requirements.
